newsitem.title: UK: Report urges cleaner meat conditions for Britain.
newsitem.headline: Report urges cleaner meat conditions for Britain.

text.p: A government-appointed scientist on Tuesday recommended cleaning up slaughterhouses and butcher shops to prevent another outbreak of food poisoning like one that killed 20 people in Scotland.

The report by Professor Hugh Pennington said animals being slaughtered should be in "an appropriate, clean condition" and that shops should not sell unwrapped cooked and raw meat if they could not keep the two well separated.
Pennington's report was commissioned after several outbreaks of food poisoning from the E coli bacteria killed 20 elderly people in Scotland late last year and early this year.

Opposition political parties immediately leapt on the report. Hot in the midst of a campaign ahead of the May 1 national elections, they said the report showed the incompetence of the ruling Conservative Party.

"There is a common thread that links all these food scandals," said Robin Cook, foreign affairs spokesman for the Labour Party. "They are the product of a government that puts its own dogma on deregulation before the safety of public food."
Labour's agriculture spokesman Gavin Strang said any Labour government would set up a food standards agency.
"We are in a situation of inappropriate enforcement," he told reporters. "It shows that after all these years we have got the legislation wrong."
"E coli 0157 is a particularly nasty organism," Pennington said in his report. "An important cause of human infection is cross-contamination of meat from animal faeces."

It causes severe food poisoning and can bring on kidney failure and brain damage in the very old or very young. The bacteria is killed by cooking but can spread from uncooked to cold cooked meat very easily.

Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth said his office, which has responsibility for Scotland, would consult on the details of the report, especially its recommendations for better licensing of food premises.
"There clearly has to be a cultural change amongst slaughter house operators and their staff," the report said.
It said separate refrigerators, counters and, where possible, staff should be used to handle raw and cooked meat.
Small shops and butcher stores across Britain could be affected. The Scottish E coli outbreak was traced in part to a butcher's shop that sold cooked steak and gravy to old people's homes.
The government has already had to fight off several scandals over conditions in British slaughterhouses.
Last month Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg was accused of covering up a report on unclean conditions in slaughterhouses. The government denied this.
The report by the government Meat Hygiene Service concluded that dirty slaughterhouses had becoming breeding grounds for E coli.
The government has itself admitted that slaughterhouses did not at first conform to standards meant to prevent the spread of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE or mad cow disease).
